builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
summary: This replaces single-pass LLM code generation and single-agent self-verification with an agentic harness that separates code production from independent test generation and execution-based revision. It costs repeated model calls and code executions per task, roughly three or more attempts plus tester-agent overhead, which increases API spend and latency relative to one-shot prompting. It can still fail because generated tests may share errors with the implementation (28.5% of analyzed failures) or provide inadequate coverage (73.1%), so independent verification does not eliminate correlated mistakes.
rationale: The reader uses third-party APIs and writes or reviews technical code, and the paper shows the coder/tester split materially improves consistency across attempts, but the evidence is from an exploratory configuration on finite element tasks, so it warrants workload-specific validation rather than unconditional adoption.
technique: Separate coder and tester agents for scientific code generation

claims.statement: This replaces single-pass LLM code generation and single-agent self-verification with an agentic harness that separates code production from independent test generation and execution-based revision. It costs repeated model calls and code executions per task, roughly three or more attempts plus tester-agent overhead, which increases API spend and latency relative to one-shot prompting. It can still fail because generated tests may share errors with the implementation (28.5% of analyzed failures) or provide inadequate coverage (73.1%), so independent verification does not eliminate correlated mistakes.

An exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass^3 on an extended FEM-Bench, versus 96.5% and 77.1% for the best single-agent harness (Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent); no model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass^3 without the split.
